name: page-object
intent: Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup.
problem: A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.
context: Automated tests that drive a user interface through a driver API - a browser (Selenium/WebDriver, Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO), a mobile app (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) or a desktop window - where the same screens are exercised by many tests, where the UI changes independently of the tests, and where the suite is expected to survive redesigns. The pattern pays off when the interface can be named in the user's terms ('sign-in page', 'product row') and the driver offers stable element lookup; it is unnecessary for a single throwaway script or when the presentation logic has already been extracted behind a humble object.
benefits: One point of change per surface: locators, waits and interaction mechanics live in the page class, so a UI change is absorbed there instead of being repaired in every test that used the old markup.
Tests state intent: signIn.logInAs(user, password) reads as the user's journey, while the driver calls, scrolling and explicit waits that implement it stay hidden.
Reuse without duplication: the same page object serves many tests, and a new test of an existing flow composes existing services instead of copying selectors.
The model is reviewable in isolation: the page API can be checked against the screens it represents without reading test bodies.
Navigation becomes typed: methods returning the next page object (or a typed result) turn a changed flow into a compile error or a failing page check in statically typed suites.
Asynchrony and driver quirks are encapsulated: the class - not every test - owns the wait strategy, retries, scrolling and the decision of what to re-query.
The suite gets a migration seam: replacing the driver (WebDriver to Playwright, Selenium to a component-test runner) changes the page classes' internals, not the tests' vocabulary.
tradeoffs: Front-loaded cost: every surface needs a class and its services before the first test can be expressed; the Leotta et al. measurement summarised by Fowler found page-object suites slower on the first test and substantially faster on later updates, so small or short-lived suites pay more than they save.

The layer bloats easily: exposing every element and every micro-interaction produces a god page object, and Selenide's critique of the field-per-element style - 26 annotated fields instead of one method - shows the classic structure collapsing under its own weight.

Assertions drift into the page object: verification and access mix, failures lose their meaning and assertion logic is duplicated; Fowler argues for assertion-free page objects and Selenium permits only the construction-time page-load check.

State goes stale: references captured once (cached elements, component roots, element handles) survive navigation or a re-render and fail later, so the class must decide what it re-queries and what it caches.

Navigation policy is a real design decision: page objects that construct their successors spread expected-flow knowledge across classes, while returning a generic context pushes it back into the tests - either way the choice is deliberate (Fowler's footnote on typed navigation).

Success depends on discipline: nothing prevents a test from reaching for the driver directly, and a leaked driver accessor or public element field turns the page object into a detour rather than an abstraction.

Framework mismatch: in suites whose framework recommends app actions or custom commands over shared objects (Cypress lists sharing page objects as an anti-pattern), the pattern must be adapted to the framework's idiom or skipped.

participants.responsibility: The one class per UI surface that knows its structure and locators, exposes the services a user performs there, and returns plain values, components or the next page object - never the driver.
A reusable fragment of a page - navigation bar, product row, dialog - modelled as its own object and composed into the page objects that contain it, sharing the same rules.
A typed accessor for one control or a repeated control, hiding its lookup and waiting mechanics (WebElement proxies in Java, descriptor-based elements in the Python tutorial, WebdriverIO getters).

The automation API the page objects encapsulate (WebDriver, Playwright Page, XCUIApplication, the toolkit handle); it is what the tests would otherwise use directly, so it stays private to the page object.
Composes page objects and components to express the user's journey, makes the assertions, and owns the fixture that creates and disposes the driver.

Creates the right page object on arrival or initialises element fields (Selenium's PageFactory, SitePrism's load, Selenide's open/page helpers, scalatest's go to); when absent, navigation methods construct their successors explicitly.

use_cases: A regression suite over a web application whose pages are exercised by dozens of tests: login, search, checkout and admin screens each get a class, and a redesign changes only those classes (the Selenium and Playwright POM guides' home scenario).
The same screens are driven by different kinds of test - functional, visual, accessibility, smoke - and the locator knowledge must live in one place that all of them import.
Mobile application suites (Appium, Espresso, XCUITest) where screens are widget hierarchies with platform-specific queries, and the page object is the only place that codifies the platform lookup.
BDD suites: Gherkin steps stay business-readable because step definitions delegate to page objects instead of calling the driver (Fowler's layering recommendation).
Suites migrating drivers or frameworks (Selenium to Playwright, a WebdriverIO restructure): the page API is kept while only its internals change.
A scripting interface over an application whose behaviour is stuck in the UI (Fowler's scripting use), or a legacy system that can only be exercised through its window.

Selenium's documented login flow: SignInPage.loginValidUser returns HomePage, so a regression suite can exercise authentication through services while locators and page-load checks stay in the page objects.
Playwright's official playwright.dev example: PlaywrightDevPage wraps a Page, owns locators for the getting-started flow and exposes goto, getStarted and pageObjectModel methods used by tests.

WebdriverIO's official The Internet login example: a getter-based LoginPage centralizes selectors and open/submit actions, letting login specs survive selector changes without duplicating driver calls.
avoid_when: Throwaway scripts, spikes and one-off checks: a handful of direct driver calls is cheaper than a class and its services.
The presentation logic was already extracted behind a testable seam (humble object, presentation model, MVVM): testing through the UI adds latency and brittleness for little value.
The test's subject is the UI structure itself (visual regression, accessibility audit, exact keyboard focus order): an abstraction hides precisely what the test observes.
The surface is trivially stable and used by a single test: the class costs more than it saves, as the first-test overhead in the Leotta et al. measurement shows.

The framework's own model replaces shared objects (Cypress app actions and custom commands with per-spec isolation): carry the single-locator-home goal into framework helpers instead of importing page objects wholesale.
Short-lived projects whose UI will be replaced before it changes twice.
anti_patterns: Assertion slum: page objects full of assertThat/shouldBe calls beyond the load check mix access with verification, duplicate assertion logic and make failures unreadable.
God page object: a class that exposes every element, every micro-interaction and the raw driver, so tests use it as a pass-through and the layer adds indirection without encapsulation.
Field-per-element declarations applied to a dynamic UI: one annotated field per item in a generated list forces code generation or hundreds of proxies for elements the test will never touch.
Selector leakage: page objects expose their locators or element handles and tests assert on them, so markup still breaks the tests.
One page object per screen even for repeated fragments: navigation bars, menus and list rows belong in component objects composed by the pages, not in copies or a bloated base class.
Test-script page objects: methods that replay one test's exact flow, including its conditional branches, turning the page object into a hidden copy of the test.
design_principles: Encapsulation and information hiding: the test knows the services, only the page object knows the UI's structure (Fowler calls the pattern a classic example of encapsulation).
Single responsibility per surface: one class per page or component, responsible for access and interaction, not for verification.
Intention-revealing interfaces: methods are named for user tasks (loginAs, payWith) and speak the UI's vocabulary rather than the driver's.
Separation of concerns: driving the UI is kept apart from deciding what a test verifies.
DRY: every locator and interaction sequence has exactly one home.
Layering and dependency direction: tests depend on the page API, page objects depend on the driver API, and a domain DSL (Gherkin steps) layers on top of the page objects.
best_practices: Keep verification in the tests; allow only the construction-time page-load check inside the page object (Selenium's rule), and provide reusable assertion helpers instead of burying assertions in pages.
Model significant elements and components, not the document structure: page component objects for repeated fragments, composed into page objects (Selenium; Fowler's panel objects).
Return plain values, components or the next page object from methods, and pick one navigation policy - page objects constructing successors, or returning a neutral context the test resolves.
Keep the driver and the locators private; expose services, never elements, and choose stable selectors (accessibility identifiers, data-testid) inside the page object.
Encapsulate waiting: use the framework's auto-waiting locators or explicit waits inside the methods and re-query per action instead of caching elements.
Review the page API for bloat and duplication: services that repeat another page's services belong in a component or base class, and a service no test uses should be deleted.

Layer a domain DSL (Gherkin steps, app actions) over the page objects rather than calling the driver from the steps; where the framework recommends app actions or custom commands (Cypress), follow the framework.
sources: Martin Fowler, Window Driver (martinfowler.com/eaaDev, 26 August 2004) - the pattern's first description: a programmatic API for a UI window that lets a client do anything and see anything a human can, hiding the underlying widgetry and encapsulating threading.

Martin Fowler, Page Object (martinfowler.com bliki, 10 September 2013) - the name popularized by Selenium: page objects return primitive values or other page objects, should not assert, and encapsulate asynchrony; cites Leotta et al. (ICSTW 2013) on maintenance cost.

Selenium, Page object models (selenium.dev documentation, merged from the Selenium wiki) - the class-per-page formulation, the rules (services not elements, assertions belong to the tests, load check in the constructor) and page component objects.
Selenium wiki, The PageFactory - the Java support library's dynamic-proxy field initialisation, lazy element lookup and @CacheLookup.
Playwright, Page object models (playwright.dev) - the class wrapper over Page with Locator fields.
WebdriverIO, Page Object Pattern (webdriver.io) - the exported-instance style with lazy element getters, designed into the framework.
Cypress, Best practices (docs.cypress.io) - lists sharing page objects as an anti-pattern and recommends app actions/custom commands with isolated specs.
